<!-- site: execute -->

CAS Monograph 16 is *From GLMs to Comprehensive Insurance Pricing: Techniques
and Challenges* (Alan Chalk, David Deacon, Montserrat Guillen and Max
Martinelli, 2025). It starts where the GLM monograph of Goldburd and others
stops and asks what a pricing team does next. This guide covers chapters 3 to 6:
measuring a model on unseen data, penalized regression, step and hinge
functions, and factors with thousands of levels. The second part,
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.qmd`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.qmd),
covers chapters 7 to 10. Table and section numbers are the monograph's.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.md`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.md):
the same sections, data and numbers, with the R package (`glm_fit()`,
`elastic_net_fit()`, `elastic_net_cv()`, `gam_fit()`, `booster_fit()`,
`family_deviance()`). Its boosting adapter calls the same LightGBM (4.7.0,
through the `lightgbm` package) with the same parameters.

**What this guide reproduces.** The monograph's case studies use data that is
not available offline (the FAA aircraft registry joined to NTSB accident
records, UK road accident counts, and a simulated auto portfolio whose rows are
not published), so this guide does not recompute their coefficients or plots. It
reproduces every worked example whose inputs the monograph prints, each with the
monograph's value beside prospicio's. To show the methods on data, it simulates
a motor portfolio with a known ground truth, as section 2.3 of the monograph
does. Models are compared by ranking and by pseudo-R2 rounded to three decimals,
because gradient boosting libraries change the later digits between versions and
platforms.

**The data.** The Python guide draws the portfolio with the numpy generator
(seed 2025), which R cannot replay. This guide reads the same draws from
`examples/data/chalk_portfolio.csv` and `examples/data/chalk_toys.csv`, which
`examples/data/make_chalk_portfolio.py` writes with the Python guide's code, so
every number below equals the Python guide's.

CI runs every R chunk that has a text block after it
(`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`) and requires the chunk to print exactly that
text, which is also the Python guide's. To render the page, install the R
package and `lightgbm`, then run `quarto render
docs/guides/glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.qmd`.

## 1. Measuring performance (chapter 3)

### 1.1 Pseudo-R2

The monograph scores every model by the share of the possible improvement in
log-likelihood that it achieves, from the null model (the mean for everyone) to
the saturated model (each record at its own outcome). Deviance is twice the gap
to the saturated model, so this share is `1 - D_model / D_null`, the deviance
explained. Table 3.1 has four records, two claims and predictions 0.2 to 0.8:

```{r}
library(prospicio)
library(gt)

y <- c(0, 0, 1, 1)
mu <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8)
null <- rep(mean(y), length(y))

# Poisson log-likelihood without the log(y!) constant, as in section 3.1.
loglik <- function(y, mu) sum(y * log(mu) - mu)

ll_model <- loglik(y, mu)
ll_null <- loglik(y, null)
ll_sat <- sum((y * log(y) - y)[y > 0])
d_model <- family_deviance("poisson", y, mu)
d_null <- family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
check <- data.frame(
  measure = c("log-likelihood, model", "log-likelihood, null", "log-likelihood, saturated",
              "pseudo-R2 from log-likelihoods", "pseudo-R2 from deviances"),
  prospicio = c(ll_model, ll_null, ll_sat, (ll_model - ll_null) / (ll_sat - ll_null),
                1 - d_model / d_null),
  book = c("-2.734", "-3.386", "-2", "47%", "47%"))
gt(check, rowname_col = "measure") |>
  tab_header("Table 3.1: pseudo-R2 of four records", "Poisson log-likelihood without the log(y!) constant") |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, decimals = 3)
```

```text
                                prospicio    book
log-likelihood, model              -2.734  -2.734
log-likelihood, null               -3.386  -3.386
log-likelihood, saturated          -2.000      -2
pseudo-R2 from log-likelihoods      0.471     47%
pseudo-R2 from deviances            0.471     47%
```

`family_deviance()` also takes prior weights, for the exposure-weighted version
of section 3.7.2.

Two more checks are arithmetic on printed values (Table 3.6 and the rebasing
factor of section 3.7.4):

```{r}
data.frame(
  quantity = c("Table 3.6, linear predictor", "Table 3.6, frequency", "Section 3.7.4, rebasing factor"),
  prospicio = c(-2.447 + 0.410 + 5 * -0.086, exp(-2.467), 0.004593 / 0.004579),
  book = c("-2.467", "0.085", "1.0031")) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "quantity") |>
  tab_header("Arithmetic on printed values") |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 1:2, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 3, decimals = 4)
```

```text
                                prospicio    book
Table 3.6, linear predictor        -2.467  -2.467
Table 3.6, frequency                0.085   0.085
Section 3.7.4, rebasing factor     1.0031  1.0031
```

### 1.2 A portfolio with a known truth, and folds from the policy number

The simulated portfolio takes the place of the monograph's case studies: 20,000
policies with driver age, vehicle age, region, power, a 300-level make, a noise
feature and a young-driver, high-power interaction. The true log frequency has a
steep young-driver effect and a rise after age 60, a vehicle-age effect that
falls until age 6 and is flat after, region and power effects, a make effect for
each of 300 makes (make sizes fall like a Zipf law) and an extra load for young
drivers of high-power cars.

`noise` has no effect. `exper` (years since the driving test) is highly
correlated with age and has no effect of its own. The chunk below rebuilds the
true log frequency from the data files with the Python guide's formula.

Section 3.7.3 recommends folds from the policy number, so that anyone can
rebuild them and all records of one policy fall in one fold. Here the fold is
the last digit of the row number counted from 0. Folds 7 to 9 (30%) are the test
data; folds 0 to 6 are the seven cross-validation folds.

```{r}
# The data files, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "examples", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}

pf <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_portfolio.csv"), comment.char = "#")
toys <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_toys.csv"), comment.char = "#")
n <- nrow(pf)
pf$region <- factor(pf$region, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"))
pf$power <- factor(pf$power, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
make_effect <- toys$y[toys$example == "make_effect"]
region_effect <- c(A = 0, B = 0.15, C = -0.2, D = 0, E = 0, F = 0.3)
true_lp <- with(pf, log(0.25) + 0.9 * exp(-(age - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(age - 60, 0)^1.5 -
  0.08 * pmin(veh_age, 6) + unname(region_effect[as.character(region)]) + make_effect[make + 1] +
  0.25 * (power == "high") + 0.6 * (power == "high" & age < 25))
pf$fold <- (seq_len(n) - 1) %% 10
train <- pf$fold < 7
cat(sprintf("%d policies, %.0f car-years, %.0f claims\n", n, sum(pf$exposure), sum(pf$claims)))
cat(sprintf("frequency %.4f; makes with under 20 policies: %d\n", sum(pf$claims) / sum(pf$exposure),
            sum(tabulate(pf$make + 1, 300) < 20)))
cat(sprintf("correlation of age and exper %.3f\n", cor(pf$age, pf$exper)))
```

```text
20000 policies, 15000 car-years, 3659 claims
frequency 0.2439; makes with under 20 policies: 166
correlation of age and exper 0.997
```

The null model is the mean frequency times each record's exposure. `cv_score()`
trains on six of the seven folds, scores the seventh and averages, for any
function that fits and predicts (a GLM, a GAM or a boosting model).

```{r}
pseudo_r2 <- function(y, mu, expo) {
  null <- expo * sum(y) / sum(expo)
  1 - family_deviance("poisson", y, mu) / family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
}

cv_score <- function(fit_predict, formula, folds = 0:6) {
  scores <- vapply(folds, function(k) {
    val <- pf[pf$fold == k, ]
    pseudo_r2(val$claims, fit_predict(formula, pf[train & pf$fold != k, ], val), val$exposure)
  }, double(1))
  list(mean = mean(scores), folds = scores)
}

# Python's list of formatted numbers: ['0.100', '0.200'].
py_list <- function(x, digits) {
  paste0("[", paste0("'", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x), "'", collapse = ", "), "]")
}

truth <- exp(true_lp) * pf$exposure
cat(sprintf("pseudo-R2 of the true frequencies on the test data %.3f\n",
            pseudo_r2(pf$claims[!train], truth[!train], pf$exposure[!train])))
```

```text
pseudo-R2 of the true frequencies on the test data 0.089
```

A perfect model explains only a few percent of the deviance of individual claim
counts, because most of each count is chance (section 3.7.1; the monograph's
perfect model scored 0.051), so compare models on the same data.

### 1.3 Null, baseline and benchmark models

The null model predicts the training mean. Its validation pseudo-R2 is slightly
negative, not zero, because the training mean is not the validation fold's mean
(Table 3.3). Rebasing to the fold's mean (section 3.7.4) makes it exactly zero.

The baseline is a Poisson GLM with age and vehicle age as straight lines and
region and power as factors (section 3.5). The benchmark is LightGBM through
`booster_fit()` (section 3.6), with the make as a plain number so the trees can
split on it. The trees see region and power as the codes 0, 1, 2, ... of their
levels in alphabetical order, in the Python guide's column order, so LightGBM
gets the same matrix.

```{r}
pf$region_code <- as.integer(pf$region) - 1
pf$power_code <- match(as.character(pf$power), c("high", "low", "mid")) - 1
f_null <- claims ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure))
f_base <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region + power + offset(log(exposure))
f_tree <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + make + noise + offset(log(exposure))
gbm_params <- list(num_leaves = 7, min_data_in_leaf = 200, num_threads = 1)

glm_fp <- function(formula, d, new) predict(glm_fit(formula, d), new)

gbm_fp <- function(formula, d, new, rounds = 150) {
  predict(booster_fit(formula, d, n_rounds = rounds, learning_rate = 0.05, params = gbm_params,
                      seed = 1), new)
}

null_cv <- cv_score(glm_fp, f_null)
cat("null model by fold     ", py_list(null_cv$folds, 4), "\n")
val <- pf[pf$fold == 0, ]
mu0 <- glm_fp(f_null, pf[train & pf$fold != 0, ], val)
rebased <- mu0 * sum(val$claims) / sum(mu0)
cat(sprintf("fold 0 rebased          %.4f\n", abs(pseudo_r2(val$claims, rebased, val$exposure))))
cat(sprintf("baseline GLM  cv        %.3f\n", cv_score(glm_fp, f_base)$mean))
cat(sprintf("benchmark GBM cv        %.3f\n", cv_score(gbm_fp, f_tree)$mean))
```

```text
null model by fold      ['-0.0000', '-0.0000', '-0.0031', '-0.0000', '-0.0009', '-0.0012', '-0.0028']
fold 0 rebased          0.0000
baseline GLM  cv        0.021
benchmark GBM cv        0.045
```

The order is the monograph's: null, GLM, boosting model.

## 2. Penalized regression (chapter 4)

### 2.1 Why fewer parameters can predict better

In the rare-car example of section 4.1, ten insurers each see one of ten cars
for a year, and one car has a claim. An unpenalized GLM at each insurer predicts
100% or 0%: right on average (10%), far off each time. The spread of the ten
predictions is the variance of the model. This is the population variance
(divide by 10), as in the monograph.

```{r}
preds <- c(1, rep(0, 9))
pop_var <- mean((preds - mean(preds))^2)
cat(sprintf("mean %.2f, variance %.2f, sd %.2f (printed 0.09, 0.30)\n",
            mean(preds), pop_var, sqrt(pop_var)))
```

```text
mean 0.10, variance 0.09, sd 0.30 (printed 0.09, 0.30)
```

A model that ignores this car and predicts the 5% average for every make has
bias but no variance, and every insurer is closer to the truth with it.
Penalized regression trades bias for variance continuously, by maximizing the
log-likelihood less a penalty on the coefficients:

- ridge: the sum of their squares,
- lasso: the sum of their absolute values,
- elastic net: a mix of the two, with weight `alpha` on the lasso part.

`elastic_net_fit()` minimizes the glmnet objective: half the mean deviance plus
`lambda` times the penalty. The intercept is not penalized and the columns are
standardized first. Its `lambda` and `alpha` are the monograph's lambda and
alpha (section 4.6.3).

### 2.2 Ridge in closed form, and why features are standardized

For one feature, a normal response and no intercept, ridge divides the mean of
`x * y` by the mean of `x^2` plus `lambda` (section 4.7.1), which pulls the
least squares estimate towards zero. In section 4.7.2 the means are 10 and 5
with length in metres, and `lambda` = 5. In centimetres they are 100 and 10,000
times larger, so the same `lambda` shrinks almost nothing:

```{r}
units <- data.frame(unit = c("metres", "centimetres"), xy = c(10, 1000), xx = c(5, 50000),
                    scale = c(1, 100))
ridge_b <- units$xy / (units$xx + 5)
data.frame(unit = units$unit, `least squares` = units$xy / units$xx, ridge = ridge_b,
           `frequency at 1 m` = ridge_b * units$scale, check.names = FALSE) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "unit") |>
  tab_header("Section 4.7.2: ridge on one length in two units", "lambda = 5") |>
  fmt_number(columns = `least squares`, decimals = 4) |>
  fmt_number(columns = ridge, decimals = 6) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `frequency at 1 m`, decimals = 4)
```

```text
             least squares     ridge  frequency at 1 m
metres              2.0000  1.000000            1.0000
centimetres         0.0200  0.019998            1.9998
```

The monograph prints 0.019 and 1.9 for centimetres: it truncated the exact
values. The units, not the data, set the effect of the penalty.

Standardizing each feature to unit standard deviation before the penalty removes
this. `elastic_net_fit()` does it by default and returns coefficients on the
original scale, so ridge on metres and on centimetres differ by exactly the
factor of 100. The 200 lengths are the Python guide's draws, from
`chalk_toys.csv`:

```{r}
len <- toys[toys$example == "metres", ]
b_m <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ x, len, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.5))[[2]]
b_cm <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ I(100 * x), len, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.5))[[2]]
cat(sprintf("metres %.6f, centimetres x 100 %.6f\n", b_m, 100 * b_cm))
```

```text
metres 1.343762, centimetres x 100 1.343762
```

### 2.3 The lasso sets coefficients to exactly zero

Section 4.7.3: for one standardized feature, the lasso estimate is the least
squares estimate moved towards zero by `lambda`, and exactly zero beyond it
(soft-thresholding). With this objective the least squares estimate is the mean
of `x * y`:

```{r}
soft <- toys[toys$example == "soft", ]
ols <- mean(soft$x * soft$y)
soft_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4), function(lam) {
  b <- coef(elastic_net_fit(y ~ x, soft, family = "gaussian", alpha = 1, lambda = lam))[[2]]
  data.frame(lam = sprintf("%.1f", lam), lasso = b,
             `soft threshold` = sign(ols) * max(abs(ols) - lam, 0), check.names = FALSE)
}))
gt(soft_rows, rowname_col = "lam") |>
  tab_header("Section 4.7.3: the lasso is the soft threshold", "One standardized feature") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(lasso, `soft threshold`), decimals = 4)
```

```text
      lasso  soft threshold
0.0  0.3382          0.3382
0.1  0.2382          0.2382
0.2  0.1382          0.1382
0.4  0.0000          0.0000
```

### 2.4 Paths and choosing the penalty by cross-validation

Tables 4.1 and 4.2 show the coefficient of log aircraft age shrinking as the
penalty grows: smoothly for ridge, to zero for the lasso. The chunk repeats this
with log driver age. For a Poisson model, records with equal features can be
summed (section 8.3), so the age-only models use 63 ages times 10 folds.

`elastic_net_fit()` with `lambda = NULL` gives the default glmnet path. The
first `lambda` of this path is the smallest that sets every coefficient to
zero:

```{r}
cells <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ age + fold, pf, sum)
cells <- cells[order(cells$age * 10 + cells$fold), ]
cells$log_age <- log(cells$age)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_logage <- claims ~ log_age + offset(log(exposure))
top <- elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 1)@lambda[1]
paths <- sapply(c(ridge = 0, lasso = 1), function(a) {
  scale <- if (a == 0) 100 else 1
  lams <- scale * top * c(1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03, 0.01, 0)
  as.numeric(elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = a, lambda = lams)@coefficients["log_age", ])
})
data.frame(penalty = c("1", "0.3", "0.1", "0.03", "0.01", "0 (GLM)"),
           ridge = paths[, "ridge"], lasso = paths[, "lasso"]) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "penalty") |>
  tab_header("Tables 4.1 and 4.2: the log-age coefficient along the path",
             "Penalty as a share of the largest one; ridge starts at 100 times the lasso's") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(ridge, lasso), decimals = 3)
```

```text
          ridge   lasso
1        -0.023   0.000
0.3      -0.067  -0.292
0.1      -0.153  -0.373
0.03     -0.275  -0.401
0.01     -0.354  -0.409
0 (GLM)  -0.413  -0.413
```

Section 4.3 chooses `lambda` by fitting the path on six folds and scoring the
seventh. `elastic_net_cv()` (as `cv.glmnet()` in glmnet) with `foldid` the
policy-number folds does this. It returns the `lambda` with the best mean
validation deviance and, for the one-standard-error rule of section 4.6.5, the
largest `lambda` within one standard error of it (positions on the path start at
0, as in the Python guide):

```{r}
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 30, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
path_cv <- elastic_net_cv(f_logage, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
cat(sprintf("lam_min at position %d of 30, lam_1se at position %d\n",
            which(lams == path_cv$lambda_min) - 1, which(lams == path_cv$lambda_1se) - 1))
```

```text
lam_min at position 29 of 30, lam_1se at position 3
```

### 2.5 The relaxed lasso

The relaxed lasso (section 4.5) separates selection from shrinkage: it refits
the features that the lasso selected with less penalty or none. In prospicio
that is a `glm_fit()` on the selected columns (section 3.2).

## 3. Nonlinear effects (chapter 5)

### 3.1 Step and hinge functions, from the printed coefficients

A step function is 1 at or above a threshold and 0 below it. A hinge is `max(0,
x - knot)`. A single step at age 30 gives `log frequency = -5.2815 - 1.4689 x
step_30` (section 5.2). With steps at 5, 15 and 30 the monograph prints four
frequencies:

```{r}
steps <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("one step, frequency", "one step, relativity", paste0("three steps, band ", 1:4)),
  prospicio = c(exp(-5.2815), exp(-1.4689), exp(cumsum(c(-4.8292, -0.6881, -0.5711, -0.6237)))),
  book = c(0.00509, 0.2302, 0.00783, 0.00394, 0.00222, 0.00119))
steps[["book / prospicio"]] <- steps$book / steps$prospicio
gt(steps, rowname_col = "quantity") |>
  tab_header("Section 5.2: frequencies from the printed coefficients", "Bands are cut at ages 5, 15 and 30") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(prospicio, book), rows = c(1, 3:6), decimals = 5) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(prospicio, book), rows = 2, decimals = 4) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `book / prospicio`, decimals = 3)
```

```text
                      prospicio     book  book / prospicio
one step, frequency     0.00508  0.00509             1.001
one step, relativity     0.2302   0.2302             1.000
three steps, band 1     0.00799  0.00783             0.980
three steps, band 2     0.00402  0.00394             0.981
three steps, band 3     0.00227  0.00222             0.978
three steps, band 4     0.00122  0.00119             0.979
```

The single step's base frequency differs in the last digit: exp(-5.2815) is
0.005082 (an intercept of -5.2809 or more gives the printed 0.00509).

The three-step frequencies are all about 2% below the printed ones, by almost
the same factor in every band, which points at the intercept: -4.85, not
-4.8292, gives the printed values and keeps the ratios between bands. Without
the data we cannot say which printed number is wrong.

Table 5.7 codes an ordinal feature (pilot quality, five levels) as five
cumulative steps. A level's relativity is the exponential of the running sum of
the coefficients:

```{r}
coef_57 <- c(0, 0.515, 0, 0.211, 0.206)
data.frame(level = as.character(1:5), coefficient = coef_57, prospicio = exp(cumsum(coef_57)),
           book = c("1", "1.673", "1.673", "2.06", "2.539")) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "level") |>
  tab_header("Table 5.7: cumulative relativities of pilot quality") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(coefficient, prospicio), decimals = 3)
```

```text
   coefficient  prospicio   book
1        0.000      1.000      1
2        0.515      1.674  1.673
3        0.000      1.674  1.673
4        0.211      2.067   2.06
5        0.206      2.540  2.539
```

The exact fourth value is 2.067: Table 5.7 truncates it and Table 5.8 rounds it
to 2.07.

### 3.2 Many steps or hinges, and the lasso picks

Section 5.2 gives the lasso one step at each age and lets cross-validation
decide how many stay (section 5.6 uses 25 equally spaced steps). Here the steps
are every three years from 20 to 77, on the aggregated ages:

```{r}
knots <- seq(20, 77, by = 3)
step_names <- paste0("age_stp_", knots)
add_steps <- function(d, at) {
  for (a in at) d[[paste0("age_stp_", a)]] <- as.numeric(d$age >= a)
  d
}
cells <- add_steps(cells, knots)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_steps <- reformulate(c(step_names, "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 25, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
cvp <- elastic_net_cv(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
i_min <- which(lams == cvp$lambda_min)
i_1se <- which(lams == cvp$lambda_1se)
kept <- knots[cvp$fit@coefficients[step_names, i_min] != 0]
cat(sprintf("%d steps offered, %d kept at lam_min, %d at lam_1se\n",
            length(knots), cvp$fit@df[i_min], cvp$fit@df[i_1se]))
cat("kept:", paste0("[", paste(kept, collapse = ", "), "]"), "\n")
```

```text
20 steps offered, 8 kept at lam_min, 5 at lam_1se
kept: [20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 62, 65, 77]
```

The cross-validation curve, with the two chosen penalties marked:

```{r}
#| label: cv-curve-figure
library(ggplot2, exclude = "layer")   # keeps prospicio's layer()
cv_curve <- data.frame(loglam = log10(lams), mean = cvp$mean, se = cvp$se)
marks <- data.frame(
  loglam = log10(c(cvp$lambda_min, cvp$lambda_1se)),
  choice = c(sprintf("lam_min (%d steps)", cvp$fit@df[i_min]),
             sprintf("lam_1se (%d steps)", cvp$fit@df[i_1se])))
marks$choice <- factor(marks$choice, levels = marks$choice)
ggplot(cv_curve, aes(loglam, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), colour = "grey75", width = 0.04) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey75") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = loglam, colour = choice, linetype = choice), data = marks) +
  labs(x = "log10 of the penalty lambda", y = "deviance on the validation fold",
       colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       title = "Cross-validation of the lasso on 20 age steps") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The next chunk compares with the truth by age (the exposure-weighted average of
the policies' true frequencies) the lasso at `lambda_min`, the relaxed lasso
(the kept steps refitted by an unpenalized `glm_fit()`, section 4.5) and a
P-spline GAM (`gam_fit()`, which the monograph uses for its spatial second stage
in chapter 8):

```{r}
grid <- add_steps(data.frame(age = 18:80, exposure = 1), knots)
true_by_age <- tapply(truth, pf$age, sum) / tapply(pf$exposure, pf$age, sum)
lasso_curve <- predict(cvp$fit, grid, lambda = cvp$lambda_min)
f_kept <- reformulate(c(paste0("age_stp_", kept), "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
relaxed_curve <- predict(glm_fit(f_kept, cells_tr), grid)
gam_age <- gam_fit(claims ~ age + offset(log(exposure)), cells_tr, smooths = "age", n_basis = 12)
gam_curve <- predict(gam_age, grid)
show_ages <- c(18, 20, 23, 26, 35, 50, 65, 80)
data.frame(age = as.character(show_ages), truth = as.numeric(true_by_age)[show_ages - 17],
           lasso = as.numeric(lasso_curve)[show_ages - 17], relaxed = as.numeric(relaxed_curve)[show_ages - 17],
           GAM = as.numeric(gam_curve)[show_ages - 17]) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "age") |>
  tab_header("Claim frequency by age: truth and three fits", "Claims per policy year") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(truth, lasso, relaxed, GAM), decimals = 3)
```

```text
    truth  lasso  relaxed    GAM
18  0.565  0.531    0.553  0.530
20  0.481  0.408    0.415  0.449
23  0.363  0.304    0.310  0.355
26  0.264  0.256    0.260  0.290
35  0.216  0.207    0.200  0.206
50  0.207  0.207    0.200  0.195
65  0.215  0.236    0.239  0.228
80  0.256  0.239    0.253  0.249
```

```{r}
cat(sprintf("GAM effective degrees of freedom %.1f\n", gam_age@edf))
```

```text
GAM effective degrees of freedom 5.7
```

```{r}
#| label: age-fits-figure
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(age = grid$age, frequency = as.numeric(true_by_age), fit = "truth"),
  data.frame(age = grid$age, frequency = as.numeric(lasso_curve), fit = "lasso at lam_min"),
  data.frame(age = grid$age, frequency = as.numeric(relaxed_curve), fit = "relaxed lasso"),
  data.frame(age = grid$age, frequency = as.numeric(gam_curve), fit = "GAM"))
curves$fit <- factor(curves$fit, levels = c("truth", "lasso at lam_min", "relaxed lasso", "GAM"))
ggplot(curves, aes(age, frequency)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = fit, linewidth = fit == "truth")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("truth" = "grey75", "lasso at lam_min" = "#F8766D",
                                 "relaxed lasso" = "#00BA38", "GAM" = "#619CFF")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 1.6, "FALSE" = 0.6), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "driver age (years)", y = "claims per policy year", colour = NULL,
       title = "Claim frequency by age: truth and three fits") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

All three fits find the young-driver slope and the rise after 60 without being
told where they are. Lasso shrinkage pulls the extremes towards the middle (as
section 5.2 sees above aircraft age 20), and the relaxed fit removes part of
that. The monograph prefers steps and hinges because the result is a short
rating table. A GAM gives a smooth curve, which you tabulate afterwards.

Section 5.8.1 links steps to the fused lasso: a step at each level is a dummy
at each level with each step the difference between neighbouring dummies, so a
lasso penalty on steps penalizes the jumps between neighbours.

### 3.3 Monotone effects

Section 5.7.2 makes an ordinal effect monotone with non-negative step
coefficients. A GAM can set the shape directly: `bs = "mpd"` is a monotone
decreasing P-spline (from scam). The chunk fits it to vehicle age, whose true
effect falls until age 6 and is flat after:

```{r}
veh <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ veh_age + fold, pf, sum)
mono <- gam_fit(claims ~ veh_age + offset(log(exposure)), veh[veh$fold < 7, ], smooths = "veh_age",
                n_basis = 8, bs = "mpd")
curve <- predict(mono, data.frame(veh_age = 0:20, exposure = 1))
show <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 10, 15, 20)
data.frame(`vehicle age` = as.character(show), fitted = (curve / curve[1])[show + 1],
           true = exp(-0.08 * pmin(show, 6)), check.names = FALSE) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "vehicle age") |>
  tab_header("Relativity of claim frequency to vehicle age 0", "Monotone P-spline against the true effect") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(fitted, true), decimals = 2)
```

```text
    fitted  true
0     1.00  1.00
2     0.89  0.85
4     0.80  0.73
6     0.75  0.62
10    0.70  0.62
15    0.64  0.62
20    0.61  0.62
```

The monotone fit bends more gradually than the true hinge and keeps falling a
little after age 6, but it cannot turn back up. A constraint hides a reversal if
the data has one, so use it where the shape is known (claim history,
deductibles), not to make a factor look tidy.

## 4. High cardinality categorical variables (chapter 6)

### 4.1 Target encoding, and keeping it out of its own fold

A factor with thousands of levels (aircraft make, city, zip code) is a problem
as dummies in a GLM: it uses much memory and gives unstable estimates for thin
levels. Target encoding, the main tool of chapter 6, replaces each level by one
number, its actual-to-expected ratio shrunk towards 1 by the credibility factor
`z = n / (n + K)`, where `n` is the level's exposure. The log of that number is
the feature.

Encoding a level from its own records leaks the target into the feature (section
6.3), so a record in fold `k` is encoded only from the other folds. Table 6.1
has one make with six aircraft in three folds:

```{r}
te_fold <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)
te_acc <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1)
data.frame(fold = as.character(1:3),
           `accidents elsewhere` = sapply(1:3, function(k) sum(te_acc[te_fold != k])),
           `aircraft elsewhere` = sapply(1:3, function(k) sum(te_fold != k)),
           encoding = sapply(1:3, function(k) mean(te_acc[te_fold != k])),
           book = c(0.75, 0.50, 0.25), check.names = FALSE) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "fold") |>
  tab_header("Table 6.1: each fold encoded from the other folds") |>
  fmt_integer(columns = c(`accidents elsewhere`, `aircraft elsewhere`)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(encoding, book), decimals = 2)
```

```text
   accidents elsewhere  aircraft elsewhere  encoding  book
1                    3                   4      0.75  0.75
2                    2                   4      0.50  0.50
3                    1                   4      0.25  0.25
```

### 4.2 The credibility constant, and the printed encodings

Section 6.6 estimates `K` as the ratio of the within-make variance (an
aircraft-year's accident count, Bernoulli at the mean rate 0.004584) to the
between-make variance, which the monograph estimates from the mean residuals of
large makes as 7.038492e-6:

```{r}
p <- 0.004584
within <- p * (1 - p)
K_est <- within / 7.038492e-6
data.frame(
  quantity = c("within variance", "K", "credibility at 1,000 aircraft-years"),
  prospicio = c(within, K_est, 1000 / (1000 + 648)),
  book = c("0.004562987", "648", "0.61")) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "quantity") |>
  tab_header("Section 6.6: the credibility constant") |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 1, decimals = 9) |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 2, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 3, decimals = 2)
```

```text
                                       prospicio         book
within variance                      0.004562987  0.004562987
K                                            648          648
credibility at 1,000 aircraft-years         0.61         0.61
```

Table 6.5 lists encoded makes at `K` = 1,024, the monograph's final value. The
next chunk recomputes them from the printed inputs:

```{r}
table_6_5 <- data.frame(
  make = c("DJI", "TEXTRON AVIATION INC", "MARLIN JOHN E", "STUMP GREAT LAKES"),
  expo = c(11900, 5483, 13, 12), ave = c(0, 0.24356, 186.59373, 223.74936),
  z_printed = c(0.9208, 0.8426, 0.0122, 0.0116), te_printed = c(0.079, 0.363, 3.266, 3.579)
)
z <- table_6_5$expo / (table_6_5$expo + 1024)
data.frame(make = table_6_5$make, z = z, `book z` = table_6_5$z_printed,
           encoding = 1 - z + z * table_6_5$ave,
           `from book z` = 1 - table_6_5$z_printed + table_6_5$z_printed * table_6_5$ave,
           `book encoding` = table_6_5$te_printed, check.names = FALSE) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "make") |>
  tab_header("Table 6.5: encoded makes at K = 1,024") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(z, `book z`), decimals = 4) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(encoding, `from book z`, `book encoding`), decimals = 3)
```

```text
                           z  book z  encoding  from book z  book encoding
DJI                   0.9208  0.9208     0.079        0.079          0.079
TEXTRON AVIATION INC  0.8426  0.8426     0.363        0.363          0.363
MARLIN JOHN E         0.0125  0.0122     3.327        3.264          3.266
STUMP GREAT LAKES     0.0116  0.0116     3.580        3.584          3.579
```

DJI and Textron match. Marlin's printed credibility (0.0122) implies about
12.65 aircraft-years, not 13, so the exposure column is rounded (the encoding
from the printed `z` is 3.264). Stump Great Lakes differs for the same reason.

Section 6.7.1's worked sentence multiplies Stump's `z` by 222.22, but Table 6.5
has 223.75, which gives the printed 3.58: the text is wrong. The table's caption
also describes AvE upside down (its values are actual over expected).

Two smaller checks come from the same chapter: the Bell helicopter example of
section 6.7.2 (16 per thousand against 4 for the overall mean, against 20 for
the GLM prediction for helicopters), and the logistic blending of section 6.7.6
at a level with no data, which should get no credibility but gets some:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("Bell: %.2f against the mean, %.2f against the GLM (printed 4 and 0.80)\n", 16 / 4, 16 / 20))
for (smoothing in c(100, 500)) {
  cat(sprintf("logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing %d: %.3f\n",
              smoothing, 1 / (1 + exp((500 - 0) / smoothing))))
}
```

```text
Bell: 4.00 against the mean, 0.80 against the GLM (printed 4 and 0.80)
logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing 100: 0.007
logistic credibility at n = 0, inflection 500, smoothing 500: 0.269
```

The second value is section 6.7.6's "about 25%" for a level with no data.

### 4.3 Ridge regression on dummies is credibility

Section 6.8.1: ridge on the dummies of one factor, with a centred normal response and no intercept, gives each level the
coefficient `n_k (mean_k - mean) / (n_k + lambda)`, a credibility-weighted
deviation from the overall mean. prospicio minimizes the mean squared error over
two plus `lambda` over two times the sum of squares, so the monograph's `lambda`
is `lambda` times the number of records. A formula with `0 +` has no intercept,
so `elastic_net_fit()` fits exactly that model. The 456 responses are the Python
guide's draws.

```{r}
lvl <- toys[toys$example == "dummies", ]
sizes <- c(1, 5, 50, 400)
lvl$yc <- lvl$y - mean(lvl$y)
lvl$level <- factor(lvl$x, levels = 0:3, labels = paste0("level", 0:3))
lam <- 0.1
fit <- elastic_net_fit(yc ~ 0 + level, lvl, family = "gaussian", alpha = 0, lambda = lam,
                       standardize = FALSE)
K <- lam * nrow(lvl)
data.frame(level = paste("level", 0:3), records = sizes, ridge = as.numeric(coef(fit)),
           `z x deviation` = sizes / (sizes + K) * sapply(0:3, function(j) mean(lvl$yc[lvl$x == j])),
           z = sizes / (sizes + K), check.names = FALSE) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "level") |>
  tab_header("Section 6.8.1: ridge on dummies is credibility",
             sprintf("lambda = %s, so the monograph's lambda is %.1f", lam, K)) |>
  fmt_integer(columns = records) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(ridge, `z x deviation`), decimals = 4, force_sign = TRUE) |>
  fmt_number(columns = z, decimals = 3)
```

```text
         records    ridge  z x deviation      z
level 0        1  +0.0456        +0.0456  0.021
level 1        5  -0.0470        -0.0470  0.099
level 2       50  +0.2407        +0.2407  0.523
level 3      400  -0.0511        -0.0511  0.898
```

The penalty does the work of the Buhlmann `K`. Credibility theory estimates `K`
from variance components; penalized regression chooses it by cross-validation.

### 4.4 Target encoding the portfolio's 300 makes

On the portfolio, the encoding follows section 6.7.2. A cross-fitted first GLM
without make gives each policy's expected count, so no model predicts a record
that it saw in training. A make's encoding is its shrunk actual-to-expected
ratio, and its log goes into a second-stage GLM with the first-GLM prediction as
offset (section 6.9). For each `K`, seven-fold cross-validation repeats the
whole procedure inside each fold:

```{r}
expected <- numeric(n)
for (j in 0:6) {
  fit_j <- glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != j, ])
  expected[pf$fold == j] <- predict(fit_j, pf[pf$fold == j, ])
}
expected[!train] <- predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ])

# Sums by make, one per make 0 to 299.
by_make <- function(rows, v) {
  out <- numeric(300)
  s <- rowsum(v[rows], pf$make[rows])
  out[as.integer(rownames(s)) + 1] <- s
  out
}

# Each make's shrunk actual-to-expected ratio from the rows in `source`.
encode <- function(source, K) {
  actual <- by_make(source, pf$claims)
  exp_ <- by_make(source, expected)
  z <- by_make(source, pf$exposure) / (by_make(source, pf$exposure) + K)
  1 - z + z * ifelse(exp_ > 0, actual / exp_, 1)
}

# Per policy: a training row in fold j is encoded from the training folds other than j
# (and other than the held-out fold); every other row from all training folds but the held-out one.
make_feature <- function(K, held_out = -1) {
  te <- encode(train & pf$fold != held_out, K)[pf$make + 1]
  for (j in setdiff(0:6, held_out)) {
    in_j <- pf$fold == j
    te[in_j] <- encode(train & pf$fold != j & pf$fold != held_out, K)[pf$make[in_j] + 1]
  }
  log(te)
}

stage1 <- lapply(0:6, function(k) predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != k, ]), pf))
results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096), function(K) {
  res <- vapply(0:6, function(k) {
    d2 <- data.frame(claims = pf$claims, log_te = make_feature(K, k), s1 = stage1[[k + 1]])
    fit2 <- glm_fit(claims ~ log_te + offset(log(s1)), d2[train & pf$fold != k, ])
    val <- pf$fold == k
    c(pseudo_r2(pf$claims[val], predict(fit2, d2[val, ]), pf$exposure[val]), coef(fit2)[["log_te"]])
  }, double(2))
  data.frame(K = as.character(K), `cv pseudo-R2` = mean(res[1, ]), coefficient = mean(res[2, ]),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
gt(results, rowname_col = "K") |>
  tab_header("Target encoding of the 300 makes", "Second-stage GLM by credibility constant K") |>
  fmt_number(columns = `cv pseudo-R2`, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = coefficient, decimals = 2)
```

```text
      cv pseudo-R2  coefficient
16           0.040         0.82
64           0.041         1.08
256          0.039         1.41
1024         0.037         2.24
4096         0.035         4.98
```

The baseline GLM scored 0.021 without make; the encoded make roughly doubles
that. As in Figure 6.1, the score is flat over a wide range of `K`, best near
64. As in Figure 6.2, the coefficient rises with `K`: a heavily shrunk encoding
needs a coefficient above 1 to restore the spread. The best score and a
coefficient near 1 occur at the same `K`, as section 6.6 expects when the
encoding is correct. The rest of the guide uses `K` = 64.

A generalized linear mixed model (section 6.5) treats make as a random effect
and shrinks it the same way. Section 6.8.2 gives the Bayesian view of ridge,
which is `bayes_glm_fit()` with normal priors.
